facts: Sanderson describes characters as “the people who do the stuff in the stories”; their actions make setting, magic, and action matter emotionally to readers [Brandon Sanderson, Lecture #9: Characters].

sources.label: Brandon Sanderson, Lecture #9: Characters

facts: Truby’s hero has a basic action: the many things the hero does can be reduced to one primary action that determines the story’s middle and acts as its spine [John Truby, Blockbuster User’s Manual].
Truby’s character worksheet asks for a single, specific desire line extending through the story and a clear test of whether the goal is achieved [John Truby, Blockbuster User’s Manual].

sources.label: John Truby, Blockbuster User’s Manual

facts: Weiland’s model makes the Lie a damaging misconception, the Want its external/perceived cure, the Need the Truth or personalized antidote, and the Ghost the past event or wound that causes belief in the Lie [K.M. Weiland, Creating Stunning Character Arcs, Pt. 3; Pt. 4].

The Want usually supplies the surface plot goal, while the Need is usually an inner realization that changes the character’s perspective; Want and Need may conflict [K.M. Weiland, Creating Stunning Character Arcs, Pt. 3].

sources.label: K.M. Weiland, Creating Stunning Character Arcs, Pt. 3: Want vs. Need
sources.page: sections “What Your Character Wants” and “What Your Character Needs”

sources.label: K.M. Weiland, Creating Stunning Character Arcs, Pt. 4: Your Character’s Ghost

facts: Sanderson’s three character sliders are likability, proactivity, and competence: likability establishes empathy, proactivity concerns motivation and action toward it, and competence concerns how skilled or capable the character is [Brandon Sanderson, Lecture #9: Characters].
A character can move on any slider; progress may be upward or downward, and an iconic hero changes little on the sliders [Brandon Sanderson, Lecture #9: Characters].

sources.label: Brandon Sanderson, Lecture #9: Characters

facts: Truby’s online class asks the writer to describe how the main opponent attacks the hero’s great weakness [John Truby, Great Screenwriting Online Class].
Truby’s manual describes the hero and opponent’s desires as competing for the same goal; the central conflict is their punch-and-counterpunch over that goal [John Truby, Blockbuster User’s Manual].

sources.label: John Truby, Great Screenwriting Online Class
John Truby, Blockbuster User’s Manual

facts: Truby’s Character Web compares every character with the hero and with one another, making differences clear and detailing how each character affects the hero [John Truby, Blockbuster User’s Manual].

sources.label: John Truby, Blockbuster User’s Manual

facts: Weiland groups five primary arcs into two Truth-driven/heroic arcs—Positive-Change and Flat—and three Lie-driven/negative arcs—Disillusionment, Fall, and Corruption [K.M. Weiland, Learn 5 Types of Character Arc at a Glance].
All five arcs share foundational ingredients including Thematic Truth, Lie, Want, Need, Ghost, and Normal World [K.M. Weiland, Learn 5 Types of Character Arc at a Glance].

sources.label: K.M. Weiland, Learn 5 Types of Character Arc at a Glance
K.M. Weiland, Learn 5 Types of Character Arc at a Glance: The 3 Negative Arcs

facts: Weiland summarizes the Positive-Change Arc as: “Character Believes Lie > Overcomes Lie > New Truth Is Liberating” [K.M. Weiland, Learn 5 Types of Character Arc at a Glance].
In the Positive-Change Arc, the protagonist ultimately uses the Truth to gain the Need and ends in a Truth-empowered Normal World [K.M. Weiland, Learn 5 Types of Character Arc at a Glance].

sources.label: K.M. Weiland, Learn 5 Types of Character Arc at a Glance

facts: Weiland summarizes the Flat Arc as: “Character Believes Truth > Maintains Truth > Uses Truth to Overcome World’s Lie” [K.M. Weiland, Learn 5 Types of Character Arc at a Glance].

The Flat protagonist starts with the Truth while the surrounding Normal World accepts a Lie; the protagonist’s actions change the world rather than requiring a fundamental inner change [K.M. Weiland, Learn 5 Types of Character Arc at a Glance].

sources.label: K.M. Weiland, Learn 5 Types of Character Arc at a Glance

facts: Weiland summarizes the Disillusionment Arc as: “Character Believes Lie > Overcomes Lie > New Truth Is Tragic” [K.M. Weiland, Learn 5 Types of Character Arc at a Glance: The 3 Negative Arcs].
The protagonist ends disillusioned with the dark Truth after accepting that the comforting Lie is false [K.M. Weiland, Learn 5 Types of Character Arc at a Glance: The 3 Negative Arcs].

sources.label: K.M. Weiland, Learn 5 Types of Character Arc at a Glance: The 3 Negative Arcs

facts: Weiland summarizes the Fall Arc as: “Character Believes Lie > Clings to Lie > Rejects New Truth > Believes Worse Lie” [K.M. Weiland, Learn 5 Types of Character Arc at a Glance: The 3 Negative Arcs].

In the Fall Arc, the protagonist chooses a worse Lie at the midpoint, gains destructive effectiveness from it, and ends in personal destruction or its aftermath [K.M. Weiland, Learn 5 Types of Character Arc at a Glance: The 3 Negative Arcs].

sources.label: K.M. Weiland, Learn 5 Types of Character Arc at a Glance: The 3 Negative Arcs

facts: Weiland summarizes the Corruption Arc as: “Character Sees Truth > Rejects Truth > Embraces Lie” [K.M. Weiland, Learn 5 Types of Character Arc at a Glance: The 3 Negative Arcs].

The Corruption protagonist begins understanding the Truth, is tempted by the Lie, and ultimately rejects the Truth and embraces the Lie for the Want [K.M. Weiland, Learn 5 Types of Character Arc at a Glance: The 3 Negative Arcs].

sources.label: K.M. Weiland, Learn 5 Types of Character Arc at a Glance: The 3 Negative Arcs

facts: Burroway identifies five basic methods of character presentation: indirect authorial interpretation plus four direct methods—appearance, speech, action, and thought [Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction].
Using varied methods, and allowing conflicts among them, can create a fuller, three-dimensional character [Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction].

sources.label: Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft, 3e

facts: Appearance is one of Burroway’s direct presentation methods; clothing, objects, features, and physical style can surface inner values and social or intellectual identity [Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction].

sources.label: Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft, 3e

facts: For Burroway, physical movement is not necessarily dramatic action; meaningful action involves a character pursuing a goal, making decisions, and being changed [Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction].

sources.label: Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft, 3e

facts: Speech is a direct characterization method: what a character says, how it is phrased, and what it avoids can reveal personality, values, and relationships [Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction].

sources.label: Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft, 3e

facts: Thought is a direct method that gives access to a character’s private perceptions, judgments, motives, and emotional response [Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction].

sources.label: Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft, 3e

facts: Burroway’s terminology is exact: appearance, speech, action, and thought are the four direct methods; authorial interpretation is the indirect method [Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction].

sources.label: Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft, 3e

facts: Burroway treats setting as more than backdrop: setting can harmonize or conflict with character, establish atmosphere, and influence what happens and how characters feel [Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction].
Atmosphere can be created through place, weather, time, objects, tone, and the emotional relation between foreground characters and background [Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction].

sources.label: Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft, 3e
Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft, 3e

facts: Fictional events necessarily occur in space and time; Burroway’s setting chapter treats boundaries in space and time as a narrative choice and setting as contextual background that can affect characters and readers [Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction].

sources.label: Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft, 3e

facts: Sanderson’s First Law: “An author’s ability to solve conflict with magic is DIRECTLY PROPORTIONAL to how well the reader understands said magic” [Brandon Sanderson, What Are Sanderson’s Laws of Magic?].
Sanderson’s Second Law is “Limitations > Powers” [Brandon Sanderson, What Are Sanderson’s Laws of Magic?].
Sanderson’s Third Law is “Expand what you already have before you add something new” [Brandon Sanderson, What Are Sanderson’s Laws of Magic?].

sources.label: Brandon Sanderson, What Are Sanderson’s Laws of Magic?
sources.page: First, Second, and Third Law sections

facts: Jo Walton distinguishes the simple infodump from “incluing”: “scattering pieces of information seamlessly through the text to add up to a big picture”; the reader connects the clues [Jo Walton, SF Reading Protocols].

Hemingway’s Chapter 16 image says, “The dignity of movement of an ice-berg is due to only one-eighth of it being above water”; the visible text should imply deeper unstated knowledge [Ernest Hemingway, Death in the Afternoon].

sources.label: Jo Walton, SF Reading Protocols
Ernest Hemingway, Death in the Afternoon

facts: Burroway frames point of view through three questions: who speaks, who sees/knows, and how much information is available; the choice controls perspective, distance, and reader alignment [Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction].

sources.label: Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft, 3e

facts: Burroway distinguishes first-, second-, and third-person narration, then subdivides third person by information access (objective, limited omniscient, editorial omniscient) [Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction].

sources.label: Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft, 3e

facts: First person makes a character the narrator, using “I”; the narrator may be central to the action or peripheral while recounting someone else’s story [Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction].

sources.label: Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft, 3e

facts: Second person addresses a character or reader as “you”; Burroway calls it unusual and potentially intimate, while noting it assigns the reader specific characteristics and reactions [Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction].

sources.label: Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft, 3e

facts: Third-person limited/limited omniscient lets the author report externally while accessing the thoughts of one character; Burroway calls it a common form and contrasts it with omniscience [Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction].

sources.label: Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft, 3e

facts: Third-person omniscient can move freely across time and space, report multiple characters’ thoughts, and offer judgments or information unavailable to the characters [Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction].

sources.label: Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft, 3e

facts: DeFreitas defines head-hopping as multiple POVs within one scene without a line or chapter break; it can jar readers by making whose mind they occupy unclear [Susan DeFreitas, How Big of a Problem Is “Head Hopping”?].
She recommends a real reason for a switch, a clearly signaled handoff, and naming the new POV character at the new paragraph’s start [Susan DeFreitas, How Big of a Problem Is “Head Hopping”?].

sources.label: Susan DeFreitas, How Big of a Problem Is “Head Hopping”?
sources.page: sections “Head hopping” and “How can omniscient POV be done well?”

facts: Le Guin’s formulation is that the fictional “past tense” is not past and the fictional “present tense” is not present; both are constructions on the page [Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft].

sources.label: Myfanwy Collins, quoting Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft

facts: Past tense can provide temporal range for narration, including retrospect, summary, and movement among earlier and later events; Le Guin stresses that its apparent pastness is fictional [Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft].

sources.label: Myfanwy Collins, quoting Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft
Philip Pullman, Philip Pullman Calls Time on the Present Tense

facts: Pullman argues that present-tense narration has a limited expressive range when used continuously, because it removes contrast with past, future, habitual, and conditional tenses [Philip Pullman, Philip Pullman Calls Time on the Present Tense].
Pullman also notes that a present-tense passage can gain force when contrasted with surrounding past-tense narration [Philip Pullman, Philip Pullman Calls Time on the Present Tense].

sources.label: Philip Pullman, Philip Pullman Calls Time on the Present Tense

facts: Gardner’s five examples move from detached historical narration toward immediate bodily sensation; psychic distance is the felt distance between reader and events [John Gardner, The Art of Fiction].

sources.label: John Gardner, The Art of Fiction
University of Nevada, Reno Writing Center, Psychic Distance in Creative Writing

facts: Gardner’s farthest example is: “It was winter of the year 1853. A large man stepped out of a doorway.” [John Gardner, The Art of Fiction].

sources.label: John Gardner, The Art of Fiction

facts: Gardner’s second level names Henry J. Warburton and reports that he had never much cared for snowstorms: “Henry J. Warburton had never much cared for snowstorms.” [John Gardner, The Art of Fiction].

sources.label: John Gardner, The Art of Fiction

facts: Gardner’s third level states the character’s feeling directly: “Henry hated snowstorms.” [John Gardner, The Art of Fiction].

sources.label: John Gardner, The Art of Fiction

facts: Gardner’s fourth level enters emotionally charged interior language: “God how he hated these damn snowstorms.” [John Gardner, The Art of Fiction].

sources.label: John Gardner, The Art of Fiction

facts: Gardner’s closest level is immediate sensation: “Snow. Under your collar, down inside your shoes, freezing and plugging up your miserable soul . . .” [John Gardner, The Art of Fiction].

sources.label: John Gardner, The Art of Fiction

facts: Narrative voice is made from the narrator’s word choice, rhythm/syntax, attitude, perspective, and level of commentary; it is distinct from the author’s personal voice [OpenStax Writing Guide].

sources.label: OpenStax, Writing Guide

facts: Lee Child says prose should “trip forward”: suspense can operate at word, sentence, paragraph, page, and chapter scale through pacing, timing, and language [Lee Child, Writing Popular Fiction].

sources.label: Lee Child, Writing Popular Fiction

facts: Burroway’s scene (“showing”) and summary (“telling”) are two ways fiction manages time: scene slows events into moment-by-moment presentation, while summary compresses a longer period [Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction].

sources.label: Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft, 3e

facts: Scene provides immediacy and drama by presenting events as they occur, including concrete action, dialogue, and reaction [Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction].

sources.label: Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft, 3e

facts: Summary compresses time and is useful for background, unimportant periods, repeated events, or moving the story forward quickly [Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction].

sources.label: Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft, 3e

facts: Burroway defines a concrete detail as one that appeals to a sense; it is significant when it also conveys an idea or judgment [Janet Burroway, Significant Detail].
Burroway argues that sensory details that matter let readers infer abstractions and judgments instead of receiving an authorial explanation [Janet Burroway, Significant Detail].

sources.label: Janet Burroway, Significant Detail
sources.page: pp. 1–2 of handout; excerpt from Writing Fiction

facts: Burroway treats dialogue as direct speech, indirect dialogue, and summary dialogue; dialogue should reveal character, convey information, create conflict or desire, and move the story forward [Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction].
Dialogue becomes dramatic action when it carries the possibility of change; talk by itself is not action [Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction].

sources.label: Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft, 3e
Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft, 3e

facts: A dialogue tag identifies the speaker; Burroway says it usually needs to do nothing more, and that “said” is adequate [Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction].

Leonard’s rules are: “Never use a verb other than ‘said’ to carry dialogue” and “Never use an adverb to modify the verb ‘said’” [Elmore Leonard, Easy on the Adverbs, Exclamation Points and Especially Hooptedoodle].

sources.label: Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft, 3e
Elmore Leonard, Easy on the Adverbs, Exclamation Points and Especially Hooptedoodle

facts: “Said” is a neutral, sufficient tag whose main job is to identify the speaker [Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction].

sources.label: Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft, 3e

facts: An action beat is a short piece of physical action attached to or surrounding dialogue; Browne and King recommend it when the action adds meaning or identifies the speaker [Renni Browne and Dave King, Self-Editing for Fiction Writers].

sources.label: Renni Browne and Dave King, Self-Editing for Fiction Writers

facts: No tag is needed when the speaker is already clear from the surrounding prose or when an action beat identifies the speaker [Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction; Renni Browne and Dave King, Self-Editing for Fiction Writers].

sources.label: Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft, 3e
Renni Browne and Dave King, Self-Editing for Fiction Writers

facts: Leonard’s Rule 4 says never use an adverb to modify “said”; he prefers dialogue whose wording and action carry the emotion [Elmore Leonard, Easy on the Adverbs, Exclamation Points and Especially Hooptedoodle].

sources.label: Elmore Leonard, Easy on the Adverbs, Exclamation Points and Especially Hooptedoodle

facts: Provost’s famous rhythm exercise begins, “This sentence has five words. Here are five more words”; it warns that repeated same-length sentences create monotony and recommends varying sentence length and rhythm [Gary Provost, 100 Ways to Improve Your Writing].

sources.label: San José State University Writing Center, Sentence Variety and Rhythm

facts: Burroway presents theme as emerging through the interaction of setting, tone, action, thought, and recurring details rather than as an abstract statement pasted onto a story [Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction].

sources.label: Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft, 3e

facts: McKee defines a controlling idea as value plus cause: the story’s final value charge and the primary cause producing that change, expressed in one sentence [Robert McKee, Story].

sources.label: How Writers Read, Controlling Value

facts: A motif is a recurring element—image, object, action, word, sound, setting, or symbol—that gains significance through repetition and helps develop a work’s themes or meaning [Oregon State University, What Is a Motif?].

sources.label: Oregon State University, What Is a Motif?

facts: Maass says micro-tension is not explosions or shouting but unease in the reader’s mind; when tension exists, the reader relieves it by reading the next thing on the page [Donald Maass interview].
Maass’s practical rule is to generate this tension constantly, on every page, so readers read every word [Donald Maass interview].

sources.label: Donald Maass, interview with Michael A. Ventrella

facts: Information gaps create reader engagement by withholding or delaying knowledge; the gap may be a question, a hidden threat, an unknown cause, or a fact known to readers but not characters [Lee Child, Writing Popular Fiction; Alfred Hitchcock interview discussion].

sources.label: Lee Child, Writing Popular Fiction
Sven Lütticken, Suspense and... Surprise

facts: Hitchcock’s bomb-under-the-table distinction is that showing the audience the bomb before it explodes creates sustained suspense, whereas withholding it until the explosion creates only brief surprise [François Truffaut, Hitchcock, as quoted in Sven Lütticken].
The commonly quoted contrast is “fifteen seconds of surprise” versus “fifteen minutes of suspense” [François Truffaut, Hitchcock, as quoted in Sven Lütticken].

sources.label: Sven Lütticken, Suspense and... Surprise

facts: A mystery gap withholds a fact the reader wants to discover—who, what, or why—and can power a novel while the answer is delayed [Lee Child, Writing Popular Fiction].

sources.label: Lee Child, Writing Popular Fiction

facts: Surprise is the short shock produced when the audience does not know the event in advance; Hitchcock contrasts it with suspense, where the audience knows the danger [François Truffaut, Hitchcock, as quoted in Sven Lütticken].

sources.label: Sven Lütticken, Suspense and... Surprise

facts: Dramatic irony occurs when the audience knows information that the characters do not, creating tension, humor, or tragedy [Magedah Shabo, What Is Dramatic Irony?].

sources.label: Magedah Shabo, What Is Dramatic Irony?

facts: Lee Child’s suspense method is to ask or imply a question and delay the answer; he applies the same loop at novel, chapter, page, and sentence scale [Lee Child, Writing Popular Fiction].
His compact rule is: “Ask a question, and delay the answer until the very end” [Lee Child, Writing Popular Fiction].

sources.label: Lee Child, Writing Popular Fiction
Lee Child, Q&A with Top Thriller Writer Lee Child
sources.page: interview exchange on questions and answers

facts: Lee Child says a first line should greet the reader with a promise, intrigue without desperation, and deliver the reader to the next line, paragraph, and page [Lee Child, Writing Popular Fiction].
A good chapter ending satisfies without satiating and usually uses a twist or revelation as a cliff-hanger to compel the next chapter [Lee Child, Writing Popular Fiction].

sources.label: Lee Child, Writing Popular Fiction

facts: Lee Child’s motto is “Write the slow stuff fast and the fast stuff slow”: compress routine transitions, but expand major action and give its details full value [Lee Child, Writing Popular Fiction].

sources.label: Lee Child, Writing Popular Fiction

facts: Ingermanson’s Scene pattern is Goal–Conflict–Disaster; its Sequel pattern is Reaction–Dilemma–Decision [Randy Ingermanson, Writing the Perfect Scene].
A Scene’s disaster requires emotional recovery and a decision before the next goal-driven Scene, creating an alternating tension-and-release cycle [Randy Ingermanson, Writing the Perfect Scene].

sources.label: Randy Ingermanson, Writing the Perfect Scene

facts: Gardner calls successful fiction a “vivid and continuous dream”; head-hopping, confusing exposition, and unexplained point-of-view shifts can break that illusion [John Gardner, The Art of Fiction; Susan DeFreitas].

DeFreitas describes head-hopping as reader “whiplash” that forces rereading and destroys the illusion of living inside the POV character’s mind [Susan DeFreitas, How Big of a Problem Is “Head Hopping”?].

sources.label: John Gardner, The Art of Fiction
Susan DeFreitas, How Big of a Problem Is “Head Hopping”?
